blocks.content: A&N Islands are one of India's foremost biodiversity hotspots for endemic species due to their long geographic isolation. This chapter is heavily tested alongside Geography (Ch.1) and Economy (Ch.4, Great Nicobar Project), so cross-reference those chapters while revising.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: India hosts four global biodiversity hotspots: Western Ghats, Himalayas, Indo-Burma, and Sundaland.
The Wildlife Protection Act, 1972 provides the primary legal framework for protecting plant and animal species across six schedules.
Project Tiger was launched in 1973 at Jim Corbett National Park to protect the declining Bengal tiger population.
Biosphere Reserves are categorized into Core, Buffer, and Transition zones under UNESCO's Man and the Biosphere (MAB) Programme.

blocks.content: A&N Islands have an extensive protected-area network relative to their small size, reflecting the high concentration of endemic flora and fauna and fragile coral-reef and mangrove ecosystems.

cells: 9 (including Mahatma Gandhi Marine National Park, Saddle Peak National Park, Campbell Bay National Park, Galathea National Park, Rani Jhansi Marine National Park, North Button Island, South Button Island, Middle Button Island, Mount Harriet National Park)
96 (the largest number of wildlife sanctuaries of any single Indian state/UT)
2 — Great Nicobar Biosphere Reserve and North Andaman/Great Andaman Biosphere Reserve (locally, the Nicobar & Andaman biosphere reserves)
≈ 86% — among the highest forest-cover percentage of any Indian state/UT

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: '96 wildlife sanctuaries' is the single most repeated numeric fact of this chapter — A&N has by far the largest number of wildlife sanctuaries of any Indian state or UT despite its small size, because most small islets/rocks are individually notified as sanctuaries.
Protection of wildlife and natural environment is enshrined as a Fundamental Duty under Article 51A(g) of the Indian Constitution.

cells: Located near Wandoor, South Andaman; protects coral reefs, mangroves and marine life across 15 islands; premier marine biodiversity site
North Andaman; protects the UT's highest peak (732 m) and its tropical evergreen forest
Great Nicobar; part of the Great Nicobar Biosphere Reserve, home to the Nicobar Megapode and giant leatherback turtles
Great Nicobar; famous nesting site of the Giant Leatherback Turtle at Galathea Bay (now overlapping the Great Nicobar Development Project area — a major conservation controversy)
Ritchie's Archipelago; protects coral reef ecosystems around several small islands

rows: Highest (No human activities or grazing allowed)
Moderate (Limited human activities and grazing permitted)
Zoned (Core area strict; Buffer & Transition allow sustainable use)
Conservation of overall flora, fauna, and landscape
Protection of a particular species or group of species
Entire ecosystem conservation and sustainable human development
Not strictly defined in all cases
Legally demarcated into Core, Buffer, and Transition zones

items: Narcondam Hornbill (Rhyticeros narcondami) — found only on Narcondam Island; IUCN status Vulnerable; a flagship endemic bird and one of the most tested species names in this chapter.
Andaman Wild Pig, Andaman Teal, Andaman Wood Pigeon, Andaman Serpent Eagle, Nicobar Megapode, Nicobar Pigeon — key endemic/near-endemic bird and mammal species.
South Andaman Krait, Andaman Cobra and several endemic reptile species found nowhere else.

Dugong (sea cow) — a marine mammal found in A&N waters, listed as Vulnerable and notified as the State/UT Animal of A&N Islands by some sources; strictly protected under the Wildlife (Protection) Act.
Saltwater Crocodile (Crocodylus porosus) — found in mangrove creeks across the islands; the largest living reptile species, occasionally a subject of human-wildlife conflict news reports.

The islands host extensive fringing and barrier coral reefs, among the richest in India, supporting hundreds of coral and fish species; Mahatma Gandhi Marine National Park and Rani Jhansi Marine National Park are the key protected zones.

Giant Leatherback Turtle (Dermochelys coriacea) — the world's largest sea turtle species, nests at Galathea Bay, Great Nicobar, one of the most important nesting sites in the Indian Ocean region; nesting habitat is now threatened by the Great Nicobar Development Project.
Mangrove forests cover extensive coastal stretches and act as a natural buffer against cyclones and tsunamis; A&N has some of the most extensive and least-disturbed mangrove ecosystems in India.

blocks.content: ★ EXAM POINT: Cross-topic exam favourite: Galathea Bay is simultaneously (a) a national park, (b) the world-important nesting site of the Giant Leatherback Turtle, and (c) the proposed site of the International Container Transshipment Terminal under the Great Nicobar Development Project — this environment-vs-development conflict is asked from Geography, Economy, and Environment angles alike.

items: Distinction between Protected Areas: National Parks allow zero grazing or private ownership, whereas Wildlife Sanctuaries permit limited rights.
Frequently asked endemic habitats: Sangai Deer (Loktak Lake/Keibul Lamjao), Hangul (Dachigam NP), and Lion-tailed Macaque (Western Ghats).
Schedules of Wildlife Protection Act: Schedule I & II provide absolute protection and highest penalties for violations.
Coral bleaching due to rising sea temperatures has affected large stretches of A&N's reefs in recent bleaching events (linked to global El Niño-driven ocean warming episodes).
Deforestation pressure from settlement, agriculture, and large infrastructure projects (notably the Great Nicobar project) threatens endemic species habitat.
Invasive species (e.g., Chital/spotted deer introduced by the British, feral elephants on Interview Island descended from logging-camp elephants abandoned after WWII) have altered native ecosystems.
Sea-level rise and post-tsunami land subsidence (parts of the Nicobar group and Indira Point subsided/submerged after the 2004 earthquake) are ongoing climate-vulnerability concerns.
9 National Parks, 96 Wildlife Sanctuaries (highest sanctuary count of any Indian state/UT), 2 Biosphere Reserves; ~86% forest cover.
Narcondam Hornbill — endemic only to Narcondam Island, IUCN Vulnerable.
Giant Leatherback Turtle nests at Galathea Bay, Great Nicobar — now a major conservation-vs-development flashpoint.
Mahatma Gandhi Marine National Park (Wandoor) and Rani Jhansi Marine National Park protect coral-reef ecosystems.
Feral elephants on Interview Island descend from logging elephants abandoned after WWII — a notable trivia fact.
Dugong and Saltwater Crocodile are key protected marine/coastal fauna of the islands.
